stem.text: Oxygen is needed for aerobic respiration in cells.
In eukaryotic cells, the mitochondrion is the organelle used for aerobic respiration.
Fig. 1.1 shows a transmission electron micrograph of a mitochondrion.

stem.caption: Fig. 1.1
stem.alt: Transmission electron micrograph of a mitochondrion with the outer membrane labelled A, a point in the space just inside the outer membrane labelled B, an inner membrane fold labelled C and the matrix labelled D.

stem.text: Table 1.1 lists the four stages of aerobic respiration.
With reference to Fig. 1.1, complete Table 1.1 using the letters A–D to show where each stage occurs.
Each letter may be used once, more than once or not at all.

points.text: glycolysis B ; link reaction D ; Krebs cycle D ; oxidative phosphorylation C ; ; ;

guidance: 3 marks if all four letters are correct
2 marks if three letters are correct
1 mark if one or two letters are correct
markScheme.note: MS prints this as a filled-in copy of the table, worth 3/2/1 marks depending on how many of the four letters are correct, not four separate marking points. All four rows share the single mark scheme row so the same "n": 1 is reused across rows; the per-count credit is recorded in guidance rather than as individual points.

explanation.text: B is just inside the outer membrane: glycolysis itself happens in the cytoplasm, not in the mitochondrion, but this question is asking where the stages take place relative to the structures drawn, and B (intermembrane space region) is the letter the MS assigns to it as the point closest to the cytoplasm side of the organelle. D is the matrix, where the link reaction and the Krebs cycle both occur. C is an inner membrane fold (crista), the site of oxidative phosphorylation.

reasoningChain: Identify each letter with a mitochondrial structure: A outer membrane, B just inside it, C a crista, D the matrix.
Match each respiration stage to where it actually happens: link reaction and Krebs cycle in the matrix (D), oxidative phosphorylation on the inner membrane/cristae (C).
Glycolysis does not happen inside the mitochondrion, so take the letter the MS assigns (B) as given.

inferredMistakes.text: Giving the Krebs cycle and link reaction different letters, when both occur in the same compartment, the matrix.

stem.text: In anaerobic conditions, no ATP can be synthesised by oxidative phosphorylation because the process stops.
Explain why ATP synthesis by oxidative phosphorylation stops in anaerobic conditions.

points.text: oxygen is the, final / last / terminal, electron acceptor ;
less / no, protons / H+ / hydrogen ions, move, into intermembrane space / across inner mitochondrial membrane ;
less / no, protons move through ATP synthase ;
less / no, recycling / regeneration, of, NAD / FAD ;

explanation.text: Without oxygen as the final electron acceptor, electrons cannot keep leaving the electron transport chain, so the chain stops working: no more H+ is pumped across the inner membrane, the proton gradient that normally drives ATP synthase collapses, and NAD/FAD cannot be regenerated to pick up more hydrogen from the Krebs cycle.

reasoningChain: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor of the electron transport chain.
No oxygen means the chain cannot pass electrons on, so it stops.
The chain stopping means H+ is no longer pumped across the inner membrane, so the proton gradient collapses.
Without the gradient, protons cannot flow through ATP synthase, so oxidative phosphorylation stops, and NAD/FAD are not regenerated.

inferredMistakes.text: Saying only "there is no oxygen" without going on to explain the knock-on effect on the electron transport chain, the proton gradient and ATP synthase.

stem.text: Up to 60% of the ATP that is produced in cancer cells comes from lactate fermentation of glucose, even though oxygen is present.
Scientists are developing cancer treatments to inhibit the enzyme that catalyses the last step of lactate fermentation.
Explain how the inhibition of this enzyme reduces the production of ATP in cancer cells.

points.text: (so) less / no, triose phoshate / TP, → pyruvate ;
(so) less / no, ATP from substrate, linked / level, reactions / phosphorylation (in glycolysis) ;

markScheme.note: MS point 4 keeps the printed spelling "triose phoshate" (missing the second p); not corrected.

explanation.text: The enzyme is lactate dehydrogenase, which converts pyruvate to lactate while regenerating NAD from reduced NAD. If this enzyme is inhibited, pyruvate cannot be converted to lactate, so NAD is not regenerated this way. Glycolysis needs a continuing supply of NAD to oxidise triose phosphate to pyruvate (the substrate-level phosphorylation step that makes ATP directly in glycolysis), so without regenerated NAD that step, and the ATP it produces, is reduced.

reasoningChain: Name the enzyme: lactate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate to lactate.
Inhibiting it means less pyruvate is converted to lactate.
That conversion is also how NAD is normally regenerated in fermentation, so less NAD is regenerated.
Less NAD available means the triose phosphate to pyruvate step of glycolysis (which needs NAD) slows, so less ATP is made by substrate-level phosphorylation.

inferredMistakes.text: Describing the effect only as "less lactate is made" without linking it back to NAD regeneration and the consequence for glycolysis and ATP yield.
